title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II
objectives: BASS-II results contribute to the combustion computational models used in the design of fire detection and suppression systems in microgravity and on Earth. Objectives Include: 1) Study the ignition, flame growth, flame spread, and extinction limits for solid fuels burning in low-velocity forced flows in microgravity. 2) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test #1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity. 3) Provide SoFIE PIs with preliminary data to refine Science Requirements. 4) Practical, realistic (thicker) fuel
summary: BASS-II burned solid materials (mostly thin PMMA plastic films, PMMA rods and SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric) inside the ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox while a gentle forced airflow blew past them. The team watched how flames ignite, grow, spread and go out in low-speed flows, and compared this with NASA's normal-gravity material flammability test (NASA-STD-6001 Test #1).
why: Spacecraft materials are approved using an Earth-gravity test. BASS-II checks whether that test really predicts how materials burn in microgravity, where the only 'wind' is the ventilation.

title: Burning and Suppression of Solids
objectives: The two main objectives for BASS are to: 1.) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test#1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity. The relation between these can be investigated by observing flames burning for the longer times available in flight. Practical, realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including wake flames which have characteristics of a fire burning behind another object (for example, a fire burning in tight area which may not be easily accessible). 2.) Assess the effectiveness
summary: BASS (the first Burning and Suppression of Solids experiment) burned practical, thicker solid fuels such as PMMA spheres and slabs, SIBAL fabric, Nomex and wax candles on the ISS. It also studied 'wake flames' that burn behind another object, like a fire hiding in a tight, hard-to-reach space, and began testing how well suppression works.
why: Real spacecraft fires start on real materials in cluttered corners. BASS links the Earth flammability test to how these materials actually burn in orbit.

title: Flame Extinguishment Experiment - 2
hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) / Multi-user Droplet Combustion Appartatus (MDCA)
objectives: The primary goal of the FLEX-2 flight experiments is to extend the results of FLEX-1 to fuels and environmental conditions that mimic real combustor conditions, as well as, provide benchmark experimental data on bi-component droplet combustion over a wide range of initial conditions in order to validate numerical simulations and to develop new theoretical models. Detailed experimental objectives can be further itemized as: 1. Investigate the role of liquid-phase mixing on the burning characteristics of bi-component fuel droplets. 2. Examine the steady and unsteady liquid and gas-phase phenomen
summary: FLEX-2 extended the first FLEX droplet experiment to fuels and conditions closer to real combustors, including two-component fuel droplets (for example heptane mixed with iso-octane). Its test plan covers oxygen mole fractions of 0.17 to 0.30, pressures of 0.5 to 3 atm, nitrogen or helium atmospheres and slow flows of 0.1 to 5 cm/s.
why: Liquid fuels and mixtures are aboard every spacecraft. FLEX-2 provides benchmark data for computer models that predict when a fuel fire keeps burning or goes out.
tables: FLEX-2 test plan (fuels and condition ranges)

title: Flame Extinguishment Experiment
hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)-Fluids and Combustion Facility (FCF) / Multi-user Droplet Combustion Appartatus (MDCA)
objectives: The FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) investigation aims to map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments, measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6, and develop reliable predictive models for combustion limits under reduced gravity conditions. The mission seeks to validate and improve simplified models by incorporating detailed chemical reactions, heat transfer, and material movement, using both space-based data and extensive ground-based tests. Key flight experiment goals include obtaining high-resolution measureme
summary: FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) ignited single methanol and heptane droplets on the ISS to map when liquid-fuel flames survive in microgravity and how well gases like CO2 and helium put them out. Its test table lists 274 tests with each test's pressure, oxygen, nitrogen, CO2 and helium fractions and how the flame ended.
why: FLEX is the backbone for choosing fire-suppressant gases in space: it shows which oxygen and diluent mixtures let a flame live and which make it go out.

title: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I
role: Prevention: large-scale fire spread in a real spacecraft
objectives: The objectives of this investigation were to: (1) determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity and (2) investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA’s normal gravity material flammability screening test.
summary: SAFFIRE-I lit a large (94 cm by 40.6 cm) sheet of SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric inside an empty Cygnus cargo spacecraft after it left the ISS. It measured how quickly a large fire grows in low gravity with air flowing at 20 cm/s, both with the flow (concurrent) and against it (opposed).
why: It was one of the first truly large fires deliberately lit in a spacecraft, which is much closer to a real cabin fire than small lab samples.

title: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II
objectives: The objectives of SAFFIRE-II are to determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity and to investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA’s normal gravity material flammability screening test.
summary: SAFFIRE-II burned nine smaller samples (silicone, SIBAL fabric, PMMA and Nomex) inside Cygnus to compare low-gravity flammability limits with NASA's normal-gravity screening test. Its table lists, for each sample, the burn length in microgravity next to the burn length in the 1-g test.
why: It directly asks the key safety question: does a material that passes the Earth test also stay safe in orbit, and vice versa?

title: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III
objectives: The objectives of this investigation were to: (1) determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity and (2) investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA’s normal gravity material flammability screening test.
summary: SAFFIRE-III repeated the large-scale fabric fire in Cygnus with two 94 cm long SIBAL fabric samples and 30 cm/s airflow, one burning with the flow and one against it, to measure large-fire growth and flammability limits in low gravity.
why: Repeating a large fire with a different airflow shows how strongly ventilation drives fire growth inside a real vehicle.

title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight
role: Detection: smoke particle sizes for detectors
hardware: Comparitive Soot Diagnostic Hardware; Refer to final report
objectives: Similar to the original SAME investigation, the primary objective of the SAME-R investigation was to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulate achieves in low gravity and to relate the droplet size distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment. One of the problems encountered during the SAME investigation was that after the thermal precipitators were returned to the ground, it was found that all the TEM grids were severely contaminated with some unidentified foreign particles, making these grids unusable although some of them showed shapes of
summary: SAME-R (Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment, Reflight) heated common spacecraft materials (Kapton, silicone, lampwick, Pyrell foam and Teflon) to make smoke and measured how big the smoke particles get in low gravity, and how that depends on smoke aging and flow. It reflew because grids from the first SAME came back contaminated.
why: Smoke detectors are tuned to particle sizes. If smoke particles grow differently in microgravity, a detector designed on Earth could miss an early fire.

title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment
objectives: One of the major goals of this investigation was to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulate achieves in low gravity and to relate the droplet size distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment. A numerical code was to be developed to predict the smoke droplet growth as a function of the fuel pyrolysis rate, the thermodynamic properties of the pyrolysis vapor, and the flow environment.
summary: SAME measured the size of smoke particles made by heating spacecraft materials (for example Teflon) in low gravity and related it to how the smoke was made and moved, with the goal of a computer code that predicts smoke droplet growth.
why: This is the starting point for designing smoke detectors that work in space.

title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator
objectives: The BRE flight program seeks to establish the burning conditions in a quiescent microgravity ambient in terms of material properties. The specific flight objectives are as follows. 1. Observe burning behavior in long-duration microgravity for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2mixtures on porous circular burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter. Consider O2/N2 ambients with various pressures and ambient O2 concentrations and pressures. NASA - considered atmosphere for human space missions will be examined: 14.7 psia, 21 % oxygen: 10.2 psia, 26.5 %; and 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen. Emphasize fuel conditions that can be relat
summary: ACME BRE (Burning Rate Emulator) used a porous gas burner fed with methane or ethylene to imitate a burning solid in still microgravity air. The objectives name the NASA-considered cabin atmospheres it targets: 14.7 psia with 21% oxygen, 10.2 psia with 26.5% oxygen, and 8.2 psia with 34% oxygen. Its table lists tests at 21% to 40% oxygen.
why: It is the experiment most directly tied to the lower-pressure, higher-oxygen air planned for exploration vehicles and habitats.

count.basis: sum of "flames ignited" over 18 test days

sources.pAtm: NASA-considered atmospheres named in BRE objectives (8.2–14.7 psia); table says pressures varied but are not listed

title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames
objectives: The objective of this investigation is to better understand the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current, analyze the dynamic response of flames to electric field changes, evaluate soot formation, and characterize stabilized near-limit lifted flames.
summary: ACME E-FIELD Flames placed small methane and ethylene flames in an electric field to study how the field and the flame's ions interact, how flames respond when the field changes, soot formation, and near-limit lifted flames.
why: An electric field can push hot gases somewhat like buoyancy does, so this data can act as a stand-in for partial gravity, which has not been tested directly.

count.basis: sum of "flames ignited" over 21 test days

title: Cool Flames Investigation
hardware: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) / Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)
objectives: The objectives of this investigation are to: 1) Examine the combustion behavior of n-dodecane and mixtures of n-dodecane/iso-dodecane at pressures ranging from 0.25 atm to 5 atm. 2) Analyze the effects of helium dilution on cool flame behavior. 3) Examine the behavior of combustion characteristics. 4) Investigate the relationship between droplet size, pressure, and flame extinction, and (5) understand the consequence of soot formation during cool flame combustion.
summary: CFI (Cool Flames Investigation) burned n-dodecane and dodecane/iso-dodecane droplets at pressures from 0.25 to 5 atm (its table lists runs from 0.5 to 5 atm), including helium-diluted atmospheres, to study low-temperature 'cool flames', extinction, droplet size and soot.
why: Cool flames burn at low temperature, are hard to see and can restart a hot fire. Understanding them matters for detecting and fully putting out fuel fires.

title: Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2
role: Detection: same smoke instrument used for dust
objectives: The focus of DAFT / DAFT-2 was to mitigate the risk for the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME). SAME relied on a commercially available condensate nuclei counter, the TSI P-Trak, to quantify smoke aerosols in a microgravity environment, however there were concerns that th P-Trak would not be reliable in microgravity as it relies on gravity to recycle isopropyl alcohol used in the measurement process. DAFT / DAFT-2 tests that a modified P-Trak particulate counter would be accurate in microgravity. Summarized objectives include: 1) Demonstrate the Functionality of the Modified TSI P-Tra
summary: DAFT and DAFT-2 tested whether a modified commercial particle counter (the TSI P-Trak) works in microgravity, because the device normally relies on gravity to recycle its alcohol. It sampled Arizona road dust aerosol on the ISS to de-risk the SAME smoke experiment.
why: Detection instruments must be proven in orbit before we trust their readings. DAFT is the 'test the smoke-measuring tool' step.

title: Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity with Comparison to BASS Experiments using Two-Color Tomography
objectives: The objective of this research was to develop and validate new flamelet generated manifold (FGM) modeling techniques for concurrent flame spread in microgravity. Concurrent flame spread presented one of the greatest modeling challenges in combustion science due to the intricate coupling between heat transfer, mass transport, and chemical kinetics near the solid-vapor interface. Traditional modeling strategies often relied on hybridized turbulence and chemistry models that were not fully consistent and failed to capture important intermediate reaction pathways. To overcome these shortcomings, t
summary: This ground-based modeling study developed and validated flamelet generated manifold (FGM) computer models for flames spreading in the same direction as the airflow (concurrent spread) in microgravity, comparing against BASS experiments. PSI lists metadata only for it.
why: Better models of concurrent flame spread help predict how fast a fire could race along a material in a ventilated cabin.

title: Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment
objectives: Objective: The objective of this investigation is to better understand the structure and stability of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity. Specific objectives of this investigation were: 1. To investigate the structure of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity to understand the stabilizing mechanisms at the flames base. 2. Determine the liftoff velocity limits for different fuels and burner diameters. 3. Evaluate the impact of fuel dilution with nitrogen on soot formation and flame stability. 4. Quantify the effects of microgravity on flame length and radiative heat loss compared to nor
summary: SLICE studied the structure and stability of small gas jet flames in microgravity, including the flow speed at which a flame lifts off its burner for different fuels and burner sizes, the effect of diluting fuel with nitrogen, and flame length and heat loss compared with normal gravity. Its table lists twelve test days with methane, ethylene and ethane.
why: Knowing when a flame stays attached or lifts off helps predict whether a leak flame would keep burning.

count.basis: test-day rows (no per-test count in table)

title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment
role: Detection: soot/smoke point of gas flames
objectives: The objective of SPICE is to better understand the complex process of combustion by observing flames in a microgravity environment aboard the International Space Station (ISS) and analogous ground experiments. Specific objectives were: (1) Identify the laminar smoke-point properties of non-buoyant jet diffusion flames under various co-flow conditions in microgravity. (2) Determine the effects of burner diameter and co-flow velocity on the luminous flame lengths and smoke points. (3) Quantify the sooting propensity of different fuels, such as ethylene, propane, and propylene mixtures. (4) Valid
summary: SPICE measured the 'smoke point' of small gas jet flames (ethylene, propane, propylene mixes) in a gentle co-flowing air stream in the ISS glovebox, testing three nozzle sizes and different air speeds to see how much soot each fuel makes.
why: Soot is what makes smoke visible and what many detectors sense, so knowing how sooty flames are in microgravity supports detection.

title: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity
role: Detection: SAME smoke data for modeling
objectives: The objective of this investigation was to use numerical simulation to explore the influence of gravity on pyrolysis smoke growth from a fundamental perspective. The intention of this effort is to quantify the differences between microgravity and Earth gravity smoke, and to identify the fluid dynamic mechanisms that cause the differences.
summary: This ground study used computer simulations of the SAME smoke data to explore how gravity changes the way pyrolysis smoke particles grow, and which fluid-flow effects cause the differences between microgravity and Earth smoke.
why: It explains why smoke behaves differently in space, which feeds into better detector placement and tuning.

title: Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction Using Counterflow Flames
objectives: By using the Flame Extinguishment (FLEX) experimental data from the Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) system of combustion science, the purpose of this grant was to conduct new simulations and ground-based experiments using ozone-sensitized counterflow flames to: 1) Develop a new diagram of the flammability limits of diffusional cool flames affected by radiation, diffusion, and convection. 2) Bridge the knowledge gap between the flammability limits and extinction limits of hot flames and cool flames. 3) Verify the phenomena observed on the ISS flame extinguishment experiments. 4) Obtain new,
summary: Using FLEX flight data, this ground study ran new simulations and ozone-assisted counterflow flame experiments to draw a new map of cool-flame flammability limits and to connect the limits of hot flames and cool flames.
why: A clearer flammability map for cool flames helps make sure a 'put out' fuel fire is really out.

title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases
role: High-O2 (up to 85%) gas flames; lunar-base oxygen levels
objectives: 1. Plan and support flight testing on the International Space Station (ISS). 2. Determine the conditions for which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane, and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames; and a broad range of Zst, Tad, and fluent flow rate. 3. Support the flight tests with advanced CFD simulations. 4. Identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that yields good agreement between the CFD predictions and the ISS measurements. 5. Disseminate the results as widely as possible.
summary: ACME CFI-G burned small gas flames (ethane, propane, butane) on a porous spherical burner, in both normal flames (fuel flowing out into oxygen) and inverse flames (oxygen flowing out into fuel), across oxygen levels from 12% up to 85% and pressures of about 0.5 to 3.3 bar, to find when cool and hot flames occur.
why: It is the only data in this set at very high oxygen levels, like those in spacesuits or oxygen-enriched habitats.

count.basis: rows in normal + inverse flame tables

title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design
hardware: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) / Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) / Reconfiguration of Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)
objectives: The primary objectives of this flight experiment are: A. Obtain soot-inception limits of quasi-steady normal and inverse spherical diffusion flames as functions of flow rate, Zst, amount of inert (N2 or CO2), and pressure for C2H4 and CH4 flames. Identify the corresponding temperatures in hot regions. Obtain similar limits and temperatures for inverse and normal coflow flames. B. Obtain detailed measurements in quasi-steady normal and inverse spherical diffusion flames for C2H4 and CH4. Determine the effects of flow rate, Zst, amount of N2, and pressure on flame temperature, size, color, and s
summary: ACME Flame Design measured soot-inception limits and flame temperature, size and color of spherical 'normal' and 'inverse' ethylene and methane flames, changing flow rate, nitrogen or CO2 dilution, and pressure. Its tables list oxygen fractions from about 20% to 85%.
why: It shows how oxygen level and dilution decide whether a flame makes soot and how hot it gets, which ties to both detection and fire severity.

count.basis: rows in normal + inverse flame tables

title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame
objectives: In order to provide the experimental data needed to allow rigorous testing of computational models at the extremes of the fuel dilution spectrum, we have the following objectives: A) Characterize the behavior of weak coflow diffusion flames of methane and ethylene, as a function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, lift-off heights, temperatures and extinction limits. B) Characterize the sooting tendencies of diffusion flames with long residence times, as a function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, gas temperatures in the soot-fre
summary: ACME CLD Flame studied weak coflow methane and ethylene flames at extreme fuel dilution: flame shape, lift-off height, temperatures, extinction limits and sooting, to give computer models hard test cases.
why: Near-extinction flames are the hardest to model and the most important for knowing when a fire can no longer sustain itself.

count.basis: sum of "flames ignited" over 32 test days

title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments-Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames
objectives: A series of experiments is proposed with the following specific objectives, in both soot-free and sooty flames, to compare with detailed computational simulation to assess transport properties and detailed chemical kinetics (including chemiluminescence): Objective A. Measure and characterize the transient structure (such as temperature and species distribution) of diffusion flames established at initially non-steady, spherical flame structures for mixtures of different H2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot-free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty), for different flow rates. Objective B. Determine
summary: ACME s-Flame studied spherical diffusion flames of hydrogen/methane and ethylene mixtures, in nitrogen- or helium-diluted atmospheres of about 21% or 30% oxygen near 1 atm, to test transport and chemistry models, including how the flames change over time and go out.
why: Accurate chemistry and transport models are what let engineers simulate fires they cannot safely test.

count.basis: sum of "flames ignited" over 18 test days

title: Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets
objectives: This ground investigation sought to increase understanding of the issues that control the large discrepancy between soot formation in 1g and in 0g flames. The objective of this investigation was to integrate computational and experimental methods to derive temperature distributions and soot volume fractions from the Smoke Point in Coflow Experiment (SPICE) data available in PSI. By analyzing over 1600 raw DSLR images and incorporating advanced soot models, the study sought to improve understanding of soot formation, oxidation, radiative re-absorption, and aggregate growth in heavily sooting fl
summary: This ground study combined computation and analysis of more than 1,600 SPICE flame images to work out temperatures and soot amounts, to understand why flames make so much more soot in microgravity (0 g) than on Earth (1 g).
why: Soot levels decide smoke visibility and radiation from a fire, both important for crew safety and detection.

title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis
objectives: The objective of this ground investigation was to use flight data obtained from PSI through NASA’s Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) to quantify how externally imposed thermal and convective perturbations regulated the dynamics and ultimate fate of already established droplet cool flames, and to explain run-to-run variability by isolating the roles of deliberate heating and unintentional drift-induced convection. Focusing on both small and large droplets, the work mapped stability windows for ignition, sustained oscillation, transitions to hot ignition and warm-flame behavior, and extinct
summary: This ground study used FLEX flight data and multi-physics computer simulations to show how outside heating and small drifting flows change the behavior and fate of droplet cool flames, mapping when they ignite, oscillate, jump to hot flames or go out. Its analyzed files include droplet extinction diameters measured at 0.5 to 3 atm and burning-rate data up to 5 atm.
why: It explains run-to-run surprises in FLEX and shows how pressure changes when a droplet flame goes out, useful for low-pressure habitats.

sources.pAtm: pressures in PSI-117 analyzed data files
